rationale: The receivables component of accruals is an established return predictor (Thomas–Zhang) and its concentration in financially weak, retained-deficit firms is exactly the documented accrual-anomaly-in-distress result, so this is a rediscovery dressed as an interaction; the rank-product form also makes the low-signal (long) leg an uninterpretable mix of low-build and low-distress firms.

NEG(invch)/at is a proxy for the well-known inventory-growth anomaly, and multiplying it by a generic leverage/sales-decline distress rank is a conditioning overlay rather than a new mechanism, with the added problem that cash-flow-statement invch is noisier and less well covered than balance-sheet inventory growth.

The supplier-financing-stress story is coherent and the expected sign deliberately runs against the standard accrual-anomaly direction (rising payables lowers accruals and is normally bullish), which makes it a genuinely informative test — but it is the third instance of an identical template, so it should be run as the representative case rather than alongside its siblings.

The economics are muddled — rising accrued taxes payable (positive txach) normally reflects higher taxable income and, as a liability accrual, reduces total accruals in the direction associated with *higher* future returns, so the stated bearish hypothesis contradicts the natural direction of the expression, and txach is sparsely populated enough to threaten coverage.

Using the magnitude rather than the sign of the residual "other" accrual sidesteps the sign-convention trap and is the most substantively novel item in the batch, though it risks proxying for accrual/return volatility and small size, so the test should be checked against a plain ABS-accrual-volatility benchmark.

Falling depreciation intensity as an earnings-management flag is essentially the DEPI component of the published Beneish M-score, and mechanically it mostly reflects declining capex/asset aging, which via the asset-growth and investment anomalies predicts *higher* returns — directly opposing the stated negative sign.
